_about: Longer 'More about this place' pages, keyed by destination id. Sections: skiing, beyond, know (plain text; *italic* and **bold** allowed; blank line = new paragraph). Describe the character of the terrain, never route instructions. sources: authoritative or local first; if a vendor is listed, list a second.

nagano.skiing:
Nozawa is a proper mountain above a proper village: about 1,000 m of vertical, from tree runs at the top to long cruisers that end in town. Austrian Hannes Schneider demonstrated skiing here in 1930, and a course still carries his name. Snow arrives from the Sea of Japan in long storm cycles, so January and February bring regular deep days, and the beech glades are the local speciality.

Shiga Kogen, an hour away, is a different animal: a high plateau of interlinked areas that hosted 1998 Olympic events, with the most reliable snow in Honshu and a quieter, more domestic feel.
nagano.beyond:
Nozawa's 13 free public bathhouses (*soto-yu*) are run by the villagers, and bathing your way down the main street after skiing is the real après. At the Ōgama spring, locals boil vegetables and eggs in water hot enough to cook them. Try *nozawana* pickles, the village's namesake greens, and soba at a family counter.

On 15 January the Dōsojin Fire Festival, one of Japan's three great fire festivals, has village men defend a wooden shrine against torch-wielding attackers. Near Shiga, Shibu Onsen's lantern-lit ryokan street and the snow monkeys of Jigokudani are an easy half-day.
nagano.know: Stay in a ryokan at least once: dinner and breakfast are included and the bath is on site. Bathhouse etiquette (wash first, no swimsuits, tattoos may need covering) matters more here than in the resorts. The old village is compact and walkable; you won't need a car.

tahoe.skiing:
A dozen resorts ring North America's largest alpine lake, from Palisades (1960 Winter Olympics, the steeps of KT-22) to Heavenly's lake views and Kirkwood's high, steep bowls.

What makes Tahoe unusual is how much **backcountry** sits right beside the resorts: Donner Summit, Carson Pass, the Mt Rose highlands and the Desolation Wilderness above Emerald Bay all have deep guidebook coverage and decades of trip reports. Storms come off the Pacific as heavy "Sierra cement" that settles fast and stays stable, and spring brings some of the most reliable corn snow in the West, often into May.
tahoe.beyond: Truckee's railroad-era downtown, Donner Lake and its pioneer history, Royal Gorge (North America's largest cross-country area), sledding, and the Emerald Bay overlook. Reno is 45 minutes away if you want neon.
tahoe.know: Atmospheric rivers can bring 2 m of snow in days, close I-80, and turn the drive into the crux. Check the Sierra Avalanche Center before anything outside the ropes; guide services and avalanche courses run all winter. Weekends are busy, so midweek is noticeably better.

lyngen.skiing: Summit to sea: peaks around 1,500–1,800 m rise straight from the fjords, and most tours end a few steps from salt water. It's a ski-touring destination first (there are no lifts), with descents above the Arctic Circle in open, glaciated terrain. Late winter (March–April) brings stable spring snow and long days. By late May the midnight sun lets you ski at 2 a.m.
lyngen.beyond: Northern lights in the dark early season, Sámi reindeer herding culture, orcas and humpbacks off Skjervøy in midwinter, saunas and cold plunges, and Tromsø's Arctic Cathedral on the way in.
lyngen.know:
There are three ways to do it, from cheapest to priciest. **Camper van or a rented cabin with a car:** most classic tours start from the road along the fjords, so this is the most flexible way to chase the weather, and how many Scandinavians do it. **A lodge with guides:** in the middle, with local knowledge and saunas included. **A sail-and-ski boat:** the top end, more of a tourist experience, using the boat as a floating hut to reach fjords without roads.

Norway's regional avalanche forecast (varsom.no) covers Lyngen. Weather off the coast changes fast, and planning around it is part of the trip.

chamonix.skiing:
Chamonix isn't one ski area but several, strung along the valley under Mont Blanc: Brévent–Flégère on the sunny side, the Grands Montets above Argentière, Balme–Le Tour at the head of the valley, and Les Houches at the bottom. They aren't linked by lift, so you move between them by bus or train.

The pistes are fine, but people come for the high-mountain freeride. The **Aiguille du Midi** cable car climbs to 3,842 m and is the start of the **Vallée Blanche**, a long glacier descent that most visitors do with a guide. The Grands Montets is the steep, glaciated freeride hill. The terrain is huge and much of it is serious mountaineering ground, with crevasses, seracs and exposure.
chamonix.beyond: A real mountain town with year-round life: climbing history (the Compagnie des Guides was founded here in 1821), museums, good bars and restaurants, and the Montenvers rack railway to the Mer de Glace. The Mont Blanc tunnel puts Courmayeur and Italian food about 20 minutes away.
chamonix.know:
Geneva airport is about an hour away by road. A guest card usually gives free valley buses and trains. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited pass also covers Courmayeur across the tunnel.

The off-piste here is glaciated: if you don't have glacier skills, hire a guide. Bad weather closes the high lifts often, so build spare days into the trip. Midwinter is cold and shady on the valley floor; spring brings long days and the classic glacier runs.

lagrave.skiing:
One old cable car, in two sections, takes you to about 3,200 m on the glacier below La Meije. From there it's roughly 2,000 m of vertical back to the village, and almost none of it is groomed or patrolled. Below the top it's all high-mountain terrain: open bowls, couloirs, cliffs and crevasses.

There are no pistes to fall back on, which is the point. On a good day it's one of the purest lift-served freeride experiences in the world; on a bad one the lift stays shut.
lagrave.beyond: A small, quiet village of stone houses facing the Meije, one of the great peaks of the French Alps. The Écrins National Park surrounds it. For groomed skiing, Serre Chevalier and Les Deux Alpes are close by.
lagrave.know:
Treat La Grave as guided terrain unless you have strong avalanche and glacier skills: getting lost here means cliffs or crevasses. Wind closes the cable car regularly, so plan flexible days and have a backup (Serre Chevalier is about 40 minutes away).

Access is via Grenoble or Briançon. The road over the Col du Lautaret is kept open in winter but can close in storms.

3vallees.skiing:
The world's largest linked ski area, about 600 km of pistes across three valleys: Courchevel, Méribel, and Les Menuires–Val Thorens, plus Orelle and Saint-Martin-de-Belleville. You can ski valley to valley all day without repeating a run.

Val Thorens, at about 2,300 m, is the highest resort in Europe and the most snow-sure. Courchevel has long, beautifully groomed runs and good tree skiing lower down. Off-piste is extensive between the lifts, but none of it is controlled.
3vallees.beyond: Ranges from very luxurious (Courchevel 1850's hotels and restaurants) to simple, car-free apartment villages. Saint-Martin-de-Belleville is the traditional Savoyard village among the purpose-built resorts.
3vallees.know:
Moûtiers is the train station for the valley, with direct TGV and seasonal trains from Paris and further afield. Geneva, Lyon and Chambéry are the airports, all a couple of hours away.

Costs vary a lot by village: Courchevel 1850 is among the most expensive places to ski in the world, while Les Menuires and Saint-Martin are much cheaper on the same lift pass. French school holidays (February in particular) are very busy.

valisere.skiing:
Val d'Isère and Tignes share one big, high area of about 300 km, with lifts up to around 3,450 m on the Grande Motte glacier above Tignes. It's one of the most snow-sure places in the Alps, with a season from late November to early May.

Pistes range from long cruisers to the Face de Bellevarde, the 1992 Olympic downhill. The off-piste is legendary for its variety and is reachable straight from the lifts, which makes it popular and also involved in accidents every winter.
valisere.beyond: Val d'Isère is an old village with a lively après scene; Tignes is a set of purpose-built, mostly car-free stations around a lake. Both are self-contained and very ski-focused.
valisere.know:
The nearest train station is Bourg-Saint-Maurice, about 45 minutes away by bus. Geneva, Lyon and Chambéry are the usual airports.

The off-piste is uncontrolled and the terrain is big: hire a guide or join a group with the local ski schools if you're new to it. Altitude makes it cold in midwinter; spring here is long and reliable.

paradiski.skiing:
Les Arcs and La Plagne, linked by the Vanoise Express, a double-decker cable car over the valley. Together they have about 425 km of pistes, much of it wide, intermediate and above the trees.

Les Arcs has steeper terrain and a big vertical from the Aiguille Rouge, and Peisey-Vallandry has good tree runs for storm days. La Plagne has two glaciers and lots of easy, sunny cruising.
paradiski.beyond: Mostly purpose-built ski villages designed for families, with ski-in, ski-out apartments. La Plagne keeps its bobsleigh track from the 1992 Olympics, and you can ride it.
paradiski.know:
One of the easiest places in the Alps to reach without a car: a funicular runs from the Bourg-Saint-Maurice train station straight up to Arc 1600.

Good value for big families and mixed groups; less so if you want a traditional village. French school holidays (February) are crowded.

portesdusoleil.skiing:
A cross-border circuit of about 12 resorts between France and Switzerland, with around 600 km of pistes. You can ski a big loop through both countries in a day.

Avoriaz is the highest and most snow-sure part, with good parks; Morzine and Les Gets are lower and wooded; Champéry on the Swiss side has the famous Swiss Wall, a long, steep mogul face. Much of the area sits between about 1,000 and 2,300 m, so low snow and rain are real risks in a warm winter.
portesdusoleil.beyond: Morzine and Châtel are year-round mountain towns with plenty of life. Avoriaz is a car-free village built into the cliff, with sleigh rides and an aquatic centre. Lake Geneva is about an hour away.
portesdusoleil.know:
Geneva airport is about 1 to 1.5 hours away, which makes this one of the easiest big areas to reach for a short trip.

Check the snow before you book, especially in early season or a warm spell: the lower villages can be green while Avoriaz is still good. Weekends bring day-trippers from Geneva.

alpedhuez.skiing:
A big, sunny, south-facing area of about 250 km, from around 1,100 m up to the Pic Blanc at 3,330 m. The **Sarenne** is one of the longest black runs in the Alps, about 16 km from the top. Off-piste from the Pic Blanc is big and varied.

The linked satellite villages (Oz, Vaujany, Auris and others) add tree skiing for storm days.
alpedhuez.beyond: Known for its sunshine and a lively, relaxed resort town. In summer it's the finish of the Tour de France's famous 21-hairpin climb, and you drive up those hairpins to get there.
alpedhuez.know:
About an hour from Grenoble, 2 hours from Lyon. The sunny aspect means good light but also softer, heavier snow on south faces in spring: ski north-facing terrain in the afternoon.

Off-piste is uncontrolled; local guides know where the snow stays good.

courmayeur.skiing:
The Italian side of Mont Blanc. The resort itself is mid-sized, with sunny, tree-lined pistes that are good on storm days. The big draw is the **Skyway Monte Bianco**, a rotating cable car that climbs to Punta Helbronner at about 3,466 m. From there, glaciated freeride runs drop back towards Italy, and the Vallée Blanche descends to Chamonix.

Treat everything off the Skyway as glacier terrain, with crevasses and changeable conditions.
courmayeur.beyond: A handsome, very Italian mountain town with excellent food, long lunches on the mountain and good coffee. The Aosta Valley adds Roman ruins and castles. Chamonix is about 20 minutes away through the tunnel.
courmayeur.know:
Turin and Geneva are both about 1.5–2 hours away. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited pass covers Courmayeur, the Skyway and Chamonix.

The Skyway closes in strong wind. Hire a guide for the glacier descents unless you have glacier skills and gear. Courmayeur often catches storms from the south that miss the French side, so it's a good backup when Chamonix is dry.

hautroute.skiing:
The classic Haute Route links Chamonix and Zermatt over about six to seven days of high, glaciated terrain, staying in mountain huts each night. Most days involve long climbs on skins, some crampon sections and big glacier descents, mostly between about 2,500 and 3,800 m.

It's a demanding trip: you need solid skiing in all snow conditions, good fitness for several long days in a row, and glacier travel skills. Most people do it with a guide.
hautroute.beyond: Few trips in the Alps match it for scenery: Mont Blanc at one end, the Matterhorn at the other, and a week of high mountain huts in between, each with its own character and a shared dinner.
hautroute.know:
The main season is roughly April to mid-May, when days are long and the snowpack is usually more stable. Huts fill up and need booking well ahead.

Plan for weather: storms can pin you in a hut or force a change of plan, so leave spare days at the end. The SLF bulletin covers the Swiss section and Météo-France the French start.

granparadiso.skiing:
Gran Paradiso, at 4,061 m, is the only 4,000 m peak entirely in Italy and one of the more approachable big ones on skis. It's usually done from a hut over two days, on a long glacier climb with a big descent.

The summit itself is a short, exposed rock section that you climb without skis. Around it, the valleys offer more touring and a quieter atmosphere than the bigger Alpine centres.
granparadiso.beyond: Gran Paradiso National Park, founded in 1922 from a royal hunting reserve, is famous for its ibex and chamois, often seen close to the huts. The valleys are small and traditional, with simple, good food.
granparadiso.know:
Spring (roughly April to May) is the main season, when the huts are staffed. Book huts ahead; weekends get busy.

The final ridge is crowded on good days and needs crampons and care. The glacier has crevasses: go with a guide unless your group has glacier skills. Turin and Geneva are the closest airports.

ecrins.skiing:
A big, wild, glaciated massif in the southern French Alps, centred on the Barre des Écrins (4,102 m), the southernmost 4,000 m peak in the Alps. Hut-based touring here means long glacier days and high summits, including the Dôme de Neige des Écrins.

It feels more remote than the northern Alps, with fewer lifts and more empty space.
ecrins.beyond: The Écrins National Park protects most of the massif. Briançon, one of the highest towns in Europe, has old fortifications and good food. La Grave and Serre Chevalier are close for lift-served days.
ecrins.know:
Most huts are staffed in spring (roughly March to May) and need booking. Glacier and crevasse skills are essential here, as is a guide unless your team has them.

The southern location brings more sun, and storms from the south can bring big snowfalls. Météo-France covers the massif in its daily mountain bulletin. Access is via Grenoble, Briançon or Turin.

vanoise.skiing:
A multi-day hut traverse through the Vanoise, between Pralognan and the Maurienne and Tarentaise valleys. Days cross glaciers and high passes at about 2,500–3,600 m, with several summits within reach of the huts.

It's a good alternative to the Chamonix–Zermatt Haute Route: similar high-glacier terrain, usually with fewer people.
vanoise.beyond: The Vanoise was France's first national park (1963) and is a good place to see ibex. Pralognan is a small, traditional village rather than a big resort.
vanoise.know:
Best in spring, roughly March to May, when the huts are staffed; book ahead. You need glacier skills or a guide.

The nearest train stations are Moûtiers and Modane. Weather days are common: leave spare time and have a plan for shortening the trip.

maira.skiing:
A long valley in Piedmont with no ski lifts at all, but hundreds of mapped ski tours on peaks of roughly 2,500 to 3,000 m. The terrain is open, varied and mostly moderate, which makes it a favourite for intermediate tourers as well as experienced ones.

You tour from a village base each day rather than going hut to hut, so you can tailor each day to the conditions.
maira.beyond: This is Occitan country, with its own language, music and stone hamlets. The food is a big part of the trip: guesthouses serve long, generous dinners, and Piedmont's wine is close by.
maira.know:
The season runs roughly from December to April, with the best touring usually in February and March. Snow can be variable because storms come from different directions; check the Piedmont regional bulletin before you go.

Turin and Nice are about 2 hours away; a car is the easiest way to get around. Many guesthouses work with local guides.

verbier.skiing:
Verbier is the hub of the 4 Vallées, a linked area of about 400 km that also takes in Nendaz, Veysonnaz, Thyon and La Tzoumaz. The pistes are good, but Verbier's reputation is freeride: steep, varied off-piste is reachable straight from the lifts, from the top of Mont Fort (3,330 m) down.

The Bec des Rosses face hosts the Xtreme Verbier, the final of the Freeride World Tour. Much of the best terrain is ungroomed 'itinéraire' runs and off-piste, so conditions vary a lot day to day.
verbier.beyond: A chalet village with a big international crowd and one of the liveliest nightlife scenes in the Alps. Quieter villages around the 4 Vallées are cheaper bases. The Rhône valley below has vineyards and the thermal baths at Saillon and Lavey.
verbier.know:
Le Châble, in the valley, has a train station and a cable car up to Verbier, so you can arrive by train from Geneva (about 2 hours). Verbier is expensive, especially in high season.

The off-piste is popular, which means tracked out fast after storms and involved in accidents every winter. A local guide finds the good snow and keeps you out of trouble.

zermatt.skiing:
Three main sectors (Sunnegga–Rothorn, Gornergrat and Matterhorn Glacier Paradise) linked with Cervinia and Valtournenche in Italy, for about 360 km of pistes. The top station at the Klein Matterhorn, around 3,880 m, is the highest lift station in Europe, and its glacier keeps skiing open into summer.

Runs are long and high, with the Matterhorn in view almost everywhere. Off-piste is big and largely glaciated, so it's guided terrain.
zermatt.beyond: A car-free village of old larch chalets, luxury hotels and excellent mountain restaurants. The Gornergrat rack railway is a highlight even for non-skiers. Lunch in Italy is part of the routine.
zermatt.know:
You arrive by train: cars stop in Täsch, with a shuttle train for the last stretch. Expect around 3.5 hours by train from Geneva or Zurich.

Zermatt is one of the most expensive places to ski. The international pass is needed to ski over to Cervinia. High wind often closes the Italian link and the glacier lifts.

saasfee.skiing:
A compact, high glacier area surrounded by about a dozen 4,000 m peaks. The Metro Alpin, an underground funicular, climbs to about 3,500 m on the Allalin, so the snow at the top is reliable from autumn to spring.

The pistes are mostly glacier cruising with huge views. Off-piste is limited by crevasses, and the other areas in the Saas valley (Saas-Grund, Saas-Almagell) add variety.
saasfee.beyond: A car-free village that feels quieter and more down-to-earth than Zermatt. The revolving restaurant at the Allalin top station and the ice pavilion inside the glacier are popular stops.
saasfee.know:
Reached by bus from Visp, which has fast trains from Geneva, Bern and Zurich. Glacier lifts close in strong wind, so plan a backup day.

The glacier is crevassed: stay on marked runs unless you're with a guide. Saas-Fee is usually better value than Zermatt, by Swiss standards.

engelberg.skiing:
Titlis rises to about 3,000 m above the village, and from the top there are freeride descents of up to around 2,000 m. The best known are the **Laub**, a big, steep open face, and the long **Galtiberg** run back down to the valley.

The pistes themselves are modest; Engelberg is a freeride place first. Much of the terrain is above treeline and glaciated near the top.
engelberg.beyond: A small town around a Benedictine monastery, which has its own cheese dairy. There's a strong Scandinavian freeride community, and Lucerne is less than an hour away for a day off the hill.
engelberg.know:
About 45 minutes from Lucerne and 1.5 hours from Zurich by train, making it one of the easiest freeride trips to reach.

The north-facing terrain keeps powder well but is shady and cold in midwinter. Avalanches are common on the big faces after storms: go with a guide if you don't know the terrain, and check the SLF bulletin.

andermatt.skiing:
Andermatt sits at a weather crossroads in the middle of the Swiss Alps, catching storms from both north and south, so it often gets more snow than its neighbours. The Gemsstock (2,961 m) is the main attraction: steep, mostly north-facing terrain with big freeride lines and around 1,500 m of vertical.

Over the Oberalp Pass, the lift system links to Sedrun and Disentis for gentler, sunnier pistes.
andermatt.beyond: An old village on the Gotthard route that has been transformed by a big new resort development, with hotels and a golf course. The Matterhorn Gotthard railway and the Glacier Express pass through.
andermatt.know:
Easy to reach by train from Zurich or Lucerne, in about 2 hours. The Gemsstock is serious avalanche terrain with few easy ways down, so go with a guide unless you know it well.

It's cold and shady in midwinter; the best freeride days often come right after a storm.

engadin.skiing:
The Engadin is a high, sunny valley with several separate ski areas around St. Moritz and Pontresina. Corviglia is the main resort hill; Corvatsch rises to about 3,300 m and has long runs and a night-skiing evening; Diavolezza has glacier skiing and a long descent across the Morteratsch glacier.

The valley is dry and cold, so snow stays light, but the snowpack can be thin and weak.
engadin.beyond: St. Moritz is famously glamorous, with frozen-lake events, the Cresta Run and horse racing on the ice. Pontresina and the smaller villages are quieter. Cross-country skiing on the frozen lakes is superb, and the Bernina railway is a highlight.
engadin.know:
The Rhaetian Railway reaches St. Moritz from Chur; it's about 3.5 hours from Zurich. A car isn't needed: buses and trains link the ski areas.

Prices in St. Moritz are high, but Pontresina and other villages are more reasonable. The dry climate means persistent weak layers are common, so be cautious off-piste.

davos.skiing:
Davos and Klosters share several separate ski mountains: the Parsenn is the largest, with famously long descents to villages down the valley, while Jakobshorn, Rinerhorn, Pischa and Madrisa each have their own character. Together they offer around 300 km of pistes.

The off-piste is extensive and varied, and the long runs back to the valley make for memorable days.
davos.beyond: Davos is a real town, home to the World Economic Forum and the SLF, Switzerland's avalanche research institute. Klosters is a quieter village. Sledging runs, cross-country tracks and the Kirchner Museum fill days off.
davos.know:
About 2.5 hours from Zurich by train. The mountains are spread out, so you'll use buses and trains between them; a guest card usually includes them.

The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak in thin winters. The SLF bulletin, produced right here, is the one to check.

laax.skiing:
Laax, Flims and Falera share about 220 km of pistes, rising to the Vorab glacier at around 3,000 m. Laax is famous for freestyle: several big terrain parks and one of the world's largest halfpipes.

Beyond the parks there's plenty of wide piste cruising and good off-piste, including tree runs lower down.
laax.beyond: The Caumasee, a turquoise lake in the forest, and the Rhine Gorge (Ruinaulta) are nearby. Laax has a young, design-led feel; Flims is a quieter, older village.
laax.know:
About 2 hours from Zurich, by train to Chur and then a bus. A good choice for mixed groups where some people want parks and some want cruising.

The Vorab glacier is exposed to wind. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the SLF bulletin.

jungfrau.skiing:
Three ski areas below the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau: Grindelwald–First, Kleine Scheidegg–Männlichen (linked to Wengen), and Mürren–Schilthorn. The pistes are long and scenic rather than steep; the scenery is the point.

Wengen hosts the Lauberhorn, the longest downhill on the World Cup circuit, and Mürren's Schilthorn hosts the Inferno, a famous amateur race.
jungfrau.beyond: Wengen and Mürren are car-free villages reached by train or cable car, with very traditional Swiss character. The railway to the Jungfraujoch, at about 3,450 m, is the classic day out; the Schilthorn's revolving restaurant appeared in a James Bond film.
jungfrau.know:
Interlaken is the gateway, with trains from Bern, Zurich and Geneva. The Eiger Express gondola cuts the trip up from Grindelwald to the slopes.

The area is lower than much of Switzerland, so snow can be thin early and late in the season. Expensive, but non-skiers have plenty to do.

monterosa.skiing:
Monterosa Ski links three valleys (Alagna, Gressoney and Champoluc) on the Italian side of Monte Rosa. The pistes are pleasant, but Alagna is the attraction for freeriders: a high lift to about 3,275 m opens huge, mostly ungroomed descents.

Heli-skiing is legal in Italy, so heli drops on the Monte Rosa glaciers are an option.
monterosa.beyond: The valleys keep their Walser culture, with wooden houses built by German-speaking settlers centuries ago. The food is excellent and prices are lower than across the border in Switzerland.
monterosa.know:
Milan and Turin are about 2 hours away. The freeride terrain at Alagna is big, glaciated and serious: go with a guide.

Storms from the south can bring big snowfalls here when the north side of the Alps is dry. Weekends can be busy with skiers from Milan and Turin.

bernese.skiing:
A multi-day hut tour through the glaciers of the Bernese Oberland. It usually starts by train to the Jungfraujoch at about 3,450 m, then crosses the Aletsch region, the largest glacier system in the Alps, between big huts such as Konkordia, Hollandia and Finsteraarhorn.

The peaks include the Finsteraarhorn (4,274 m), the highest in the Bernese Alps. The terrain is high, glaciated and remote.
bernese.beyond: The Aletsch glacier is part of a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the scale of the ice is unlike anywhere else in the Alps. Starting a ski tour from a railway station inside a mountain is part of the appeal.
bernese.know:
The main season is roughly April to May. Book huts well ahead. Glacier travel skills, crampons and ice axe are needed, or a guide.

Weather comes in fast up here, and whiteouts on the big glaciers are serious. Leave spare days and check the SLF bulletin.

arlberg.skiing:
The Arlberg links St. Anton, St. Christoph, Stuben, Lech, Zürs and Warth-Schröcken into one of the biggest areas in Austria, with around 300 km of runs. It's known for steep, challenging terrain and for its **ski routes**: marked, avalanche-controlled runs that are never groomed, somewhere between a piste and off-piste.

The off-piste from the Valluga and around Lech and Zürs is huge, varied and among the best lift-served freeride in the Alps.
arlberg.beyond: The Arlberg is where modern ski technique and teaching began, in the early 20th century. St. Anton has one of the liveliest après scenes in the Alps; Lech and Zürs are quieter and more exclusive, with excellent hotels and restaurants.
arlberg.know:
St. Anton has its own train station on the main line between Zurich and Innsbruck, about 2.5 hours from Zurich and 1 hour from Innsbruck.

Lech limits how many day passes it sells, which keeps it uncrowded. The ski routes aren't patrolled like pistes, and the off-piste is uncontrolled: go with a guide to explore. It's a very snowy area, and avalanche danger can be high after storms.

ischgl.skiing:
The Silvretta Arena links Ischgl in Austria with Samnaun in Switzerland, with around 240 km of pistes. Most of the skiing is above about 2,000 m, high and open, so the snow is reliable from late November to the end of April.

The terrain suits confident intermediates best: long, wide reds and blues with big views. There is good off-piste between the lifts.
ischgl.beyond: Ischgl is famous for its party scene and for the big open-air concerts that open and close the season. Samnaun, on the Swiss side, is duty-free. Galtür, further up the Paznaun valley, is a much quieter base.
ischgl.know:
Innsbruck is about 1.5 hours away; Landeck is the nearest train station, with buses up the valley. Ischgl is busy and not cheap, especially in high season.

The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak in thin winters, so be careful off-piste, and check the Tyrol avalanche bulletin.

otztal.skiing:
Two very different resorts in one long valley. **Sölden** is big and lively, with two glaciers and three peaks above 3,000 m reachable by lift; it hosts the opening race of the World Cup season each October. **Obergurgl-Hochgurgl**, at about 1,900 m, is high, quiet and snow-sure, with mostly easy and intermediate terrain.

Together they make the Ötztal one of the most reliable places to ski in Austria.
otztal.beyond: Sölden is a party town; Obergurgl is calm and family-oriented. The Aqua Dome spa in Längenfeld is a good rest-day stop, and the 007 Elements exhibition sits on the Gaislachkogl summit.
otztal.know:
About 1 hour from Innsbruck by car or bus. Obergurgl and Sölden are on different lift passes, though combined passes exist.

The glacier terrain makes early and late season possible, but the glaciers close in strong wind. Off-piste is uncontrolled and the snowpack is often weak; check the Tyrol bulletin.

kitzbuhel.skiing:
KitzSki covers around 230 km of pistes on several mountains around Kitzbühel, and the neighbouring SkiWelt Wilder Kaiser–Brixental adds a similar amount. Runs are long, varied and mostly intermediate, with lots of mountain huts.

The Streif, home of the Hahnenkamm downhill each January, is the most famous race course in the world. The resorts sit fairly low (mostly under 2,000 m), so snowmaking matters and the season can be short in a warm winter.
kitzbuhel.beyond: Kitzbühel is a pretty medieval town with good shops, restaurants and nightlife. The Hahnenkamm race weekend is a huge party.
kitzbuhel.know:
Salzburg and Innsbruck are about 1 hour away, Munich about 1.5 hours, and the town has its own train station.

Check the snow before booking early or late in the season. January race week is busy and expensive.

zillertal.skiing:
The Zillertal is a valley of several linked and separate ski areas covered by one pass, with more than 500 km of pistes in total. **Mayrhofen** has the Penken and the Harakiri, one of the steepest groomed runs in Austria. **Hintertux** has year-round glacier skiing up to about 3,250 m.

The Zillertal Arena, Hochfügen and Hochzillertal add plenty of variety, from easy cruising to good freeride.
zillertal.beyond: Lively valley towns with lots of après and a steam railway along the valley floor in summer. Innsbruck is close for a city day.
zillertal.know:
Jenbach is the main train station, about 1 hour from Innsbruck, with the Zillertalbahn running up the valley. A car or the ski buses link the areas.

The lower areas can be thin in a warm winter, but Hintertux almost always has snow. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the Tyrol bulletin.

saalbach.skiing:
The Skicircus links Saalbach, Hinterglemm, Leogang and Fieberbrunn into about 270 km of pistes. You can ski a full circuit around the valley in either direction, which makes it great for intermediate skiers who like covering distance.

Fieberbrunn hosts a Freeride World Tour stop and catches more snow than the rest. Saalbach hosted the Alpine World Ski Championships in 2025.
saalbach.beyond: Famous for its après, with busy mountain huts and bars in both villages. Zell am See, with its frozen lake, is close by.
saalbach.know:
Salzburg is about 1.5 hours away. The area is mid-altitude, mostly below about 2,100 m, so conditions vary with the winter; snowmaking is extensive.

Good value for a big area, and popular with groups.

dolomiti.skiing:
Dolomiti Superski is one pass covering about 12 valleys and around 1,200 km of pistes, including Val Gardena, Alta Badia, Arabba and Cortina d'Ampezzo. The **Sella Ronda** is the classic: a loop around the Sella massif, skiable in either direction in a day.

The skiing is mostly groomed and intermediate, among dramatic pale limestone towers. The Marmolada glacier and the long run through the Hidden Valley from Lagazuoi are highlights.
dolomiti.beyond: The food is a big part of the trip: mountain huts serve excellent South Tyrolean and Italian cooking, and Alta Badia has several Michelin-starred restaurants. The Ladin culture, the open-air WWI museums along the old front line, and Cortina (an Olympic host in 1956 and 2026) add depth.
dolomiti.know:
Venice, Verona and Innsbruck are 2 to 3 hours away. A car helps, though buses link the valleys.

Natural snowfall can be thin, but snowmaking is excellent and the pistes are usually in great shape. Off-piste is limited and often steep and rocky: the Dolomites are a groomed-skiing and touring destination more than a freeride one.

livigno.skiing:
Livigno sits high, at around 1,800 m, in a remote valley near the Swiss border, so it's cold and snow-sure. Two sides of the valley, Mottolino and Carosello, offer about 115 km of mostly wide, open intermediate pistes and some of the best terrain parks in Italy.

Livigno hosted the freestyle and snowboard events of the 2026 Winter Olympics.
livigno.beyond: Livigno is duty-free, so fuel, alcohol and shopping are cheaper. The town is long and lively. Bormio, with its thermal baths, is close by.
livigno.know:
Remote to reach: about 3 to 3.5 hours from Milan or Zurich, via a toll tunnel from Switzerland or a high pass from Italy that can close in storms.

The altitude makes it cold in midwinter. Off-piste is uncontrolled; check the regional bulletin.

silvretta.skiing:
Gentle, glaciated hut touring on the border between Austria and Switzerland, with lots of peaks around 3,000 m. Big huts such as the Jamtalhütte and Wiesbadener Hütte make good bases, and Piz Buin (3,312 m) is the best-known summit.

The terrain is friendlier than many high Alpine areas, which makes it a good first hut trip, though the glaciers still need care.
silvretta.beyond: The huts are comfortable by Alpine standards, with good food and a sociable atmosphere. The Rätikon, to the west, adds limestone peaks and the Lünersee.
silvretta.know:
The usual starting points are Galtür, in the Paznaun valley, and the Montafon. Huts are staffed in spring (roughly February to May) and need booking, especially at Easter.

Glacier skills or a guide are needed for the higher tours. Check the Tyrol and Vorarlberg avalanche bulletins.

otztalhuts.skiing:
High, glaciated hut touring from Vent, a small village at about 1,900 m at the head of the Ötztal. The huts sit high among big glaciers, and the Wildspitze (3,768 m), Austria's second-highest peak, is the classic summit. Days are long, with big glacier crossings.

It's more serious than the Silvretta or Stubai, with greater distances and altitude.
otztalhuts.beyond: Ötzi, the 5,000-year-old iceman, was found on a glacier pass near here in 1991. Vent is tiny and quiet, and the Aqua Dome spa down the valley is a good finish.
otztalhuts.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. Book huts ahead. You need glacier skills, crampons and good fitness, or a guide.

About 1.5 hours from Innsbruck. The inner-Alpine snowpack can be weak; check the Tyrol bulletin daily.

stubai.skiing:
The Stubai Alps have one of the densest hut networks in Austria, with huts such as the Franz-Senn and Amberger as bases for lots of 3,000 m peaks. You can tour from one hut for several days or link several huts together.

The Zuckerhütl (3,507 m) is the highest summit. The Stubai Glacier ski area is close by for a warm-up day.
stubai.beyond: Innsbruck is less than an hour away, so a city day is easy. The huts are traditional and welcoming, and the valley villages are quiet.
stubai.know:
Spring is the main season. Book huts ahead, especially at weekends and Easter.

The terrain mixes glaciers and steep slopes, so glacier skills or a guide are needed. The Tyrol bulletin covers the area.

ortler.skiing:
High, glaciated touring in the Stelvio National Park, around the Ortler and Cevedale groups. Huts such as the Casati sit above 3,200 m, close to big, rounded glacier summits like the Cevedale (3,769 m) and Palon de la Mare (3,703 m). The Ortler itself (3,905 m) is more of a mountaineering objective.

The altitude keeps the snow good late into spring.
ortler.beyond: The Stelvio National Park is one of the largest in the Alps. The area was on the front line of the First World War, and traces of it are still visible. Bormio, with its thermal baths, is close.
ortler.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. You need glacier skills, crampons and acclimatisation for the altitude, or a guide.

Access is from Santa Caterina Valfurva or Solda. Milan is about 3.5 hours away.

fanes.skiing:
Quieter Dolomites touring through the Fanes-Senes-Braies nature park: high limestone plateaus, gentle valleys and some steeper peaks. Rifugi such as Fanes, Lavarella and Sennes make bases for day tours or a multi-day traverse.

The terrain is generally moderate, which makes it a good introduction to Dolomites touring, though some peaks are steep and rocky.
fanes.beyond: The rifugi serve excellent food. The area is full of Ladin legends about the lost Kingdom of Fanes, and the Lago di Braies is on the edge of the park.
fanes.know:
Access is from San Vigilio di Marebbe and the Pederü hut, with snowcat taxis to some rifugi. Rifugi open in winter and spring; book ahead.

The Dolomites' snowpack is often thin and weak: check the avalanche bulletin carefully.

julianalps.skiing:
Slovenia's Julian Alps catch heavy snowfall from the Adriatic and offer limestone karst terrain unlike anywhere else in the Alps. Kanin, above Bovec, has lifts linking to Sella Nevea in Italy and gives access to touring and freeride terrain, though its lifts have had long closures in recent years, so check before you go.

Triglav (2,864 m), Slovenia's highest peak, is a more serious goal.
julianalps.beyond: The Soča valley is famous for its emerald river, and Bovec is a small outdoor town. Ljubljana and Lake Bled are within reach for days off.
julianalps.know:
Many mountain huts are closed in winter, so tours are often day trips from the valley. Ljubljana is about 2 hours away; Trieste and Venice are close too.

The karst terrain hides holes and drops: go with a local guide. Slovenia's avalanche bulletin is published by ARSO.

whistler.skiing:
Two big mountains, Whistler and Blackcomb, linked at the top by the Peak 2 Peak gondola, make this the largest ski area in North America, with more than 200 marked runs and about 1,600 m of vertical. Above the trees are wide alpine bowls and glaciers; below them, long groomers and good tree skiing for storm days.

The coastal location brings lots of snow, but also mild storms: it can be rain at the village while it dumps up top.
whistler.beyond: A busy, pedestrian village with every kind of restaurant, bar and shop. The Sea-to-Sky Highway from Vancouver is one of the most scenic drives anywhere, and Vancouver itself is easy to add to the trip.
whistler.know:
About 2 hours by road from Vancouver airport, with regular shuttle buses. It's busy and expensive, especially at weekends and holidays, when lift lines can be long.

Check the freezing level: when it's high, ski the alpine and avoid the lower runs. Avalanche Canada covers the backcountry; the resort's own terrain is controlled.

mammoth.skiing:
Mammoth Mountain is a dormant volcano rising to about 3,370 m, with wide, open bowls up top and trees lower down. The altitude and Sierra storms give it one of the longest seasons in the US, often running into late May or June.

The terrain suits every level, from gentle groomers to steep chutes off the summit. June Mountain, nearby, is smaller and quieter.
mammoth.beyond: The town of Mammoth Lakes is relaxed and outdoorsy. The Eastern Sierra around it has natural hot springs, huge desert views, and world-class backcountry skiing in spring.
mammoth.know:
About 5 to 6 hours' drive from Los Angeles; there are also seasonal flights to Bishop. Weekends fill with Southern California crowds.

Strong winds often close the upper lifts. Sierra storms can drop huge amounts of heavy snow in a few days, then clear to sun. The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center covers the backcountry.

cottonwoods.skiing:
Four resorts in two canyons just outside Salt Lake City: **Alta** (skiers only) and **Snowbird** in Little Cottonwood, **Brighton** and **Solitude** in Big Cottonwood. They're famous for light, deep and frequent snow, and for steep, challenging terrain.

Alta and Snowbird can be skied together on a combined ticket. Storm days here are among the best lift-served powder days anywhere.
cottonwoods.beyond: Salt Lake City is close, with good restaurants and an airport about 40 minutes away. The canyons themselves are quiet; Snowbird and Alta have lodges, and the city offers more choice.
cottonwoods.know:
The canyon roads are the main headache: heavy traffic on powder days and frequent closures for avalanche control. During 'interlodge' closures, people in Little Cottonwood must stay indoors. Leave early, or stay in the canyon.

Utah's liquor laws are different from most places, but easy to work with. The Utah Avalanche Center forecasts daily; the backcountry here is serious terrain.

parkcity.skiing:
Park City Mountain is one of the largest single ski areas in the US, with a huge range of terrain from groomers to bowls. Next door, **Deer Valley** is skiers-only and known for perfectly groomed runs and attentive service.

The snow is good by most standards, though not as deep as in the Cottonwood Canyons. Many visitors combine both.
parkcity.beyond: Park City is a real town with a historic Main Street from its silver-mining days, lots of restaurants and nightlife. The Utah Olympic Park, from the 2002 Games, is just outside town.
parkcity.know:
About 40 minutes from Salt Lake City airport, with shuttles; you don't need a car in town. Prices are high, especially at Deer Valley.

The Utah Avalanche Center covers the backcountry beyond the resort boundaries, which sees accidents most winters.

jackson.skiing:
Jackson Hole is steep and big, with about 1,260 m of continuous vertical from the top of the Aerial Tram. It's famous for expert terrain, including the entrance to **Corbet's Couloir**, and for sidecountry reachable through gates at the boundary.

There's enough intermediate terrain for mixed groups, but the reputation is earned on the steeps. Grand Targhee, over Teton Pass, gets more snow and has a mellower feel.
jackson.beyond: The town of Jackson keeps its Western character, with good restaurants and bars. Grand Teton National Park is next door, and winter trips into Yellowstone by snowcoach are possible. In winter, thousands of elk gather at the National Elk Refuge.
jackson.know:
Jackson Hole airport is inside the national park, about 30 minutes away, with direct flights from several US cities in winter.

The sidecountry beyond the gates is uncontrolled backcountry: you need avalanche gear, skills and a partner, or a guide. The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecasts daily.

bigsky.skiing:
Big Sky covers a huge area of terrain around Lone Peak (about 3,400 m), where a tram climbs to the summit and opens steep, serious lines. The rest of the mountain has long groomers, bowls and trees, and lift lines are short by US standards.

The snowpack is continental: cold, dry snow, but with weak layers that make the backcountry tricky.
bigsky.beyond: Big Sky is a resort village rather than a town, but Bozeman, about an hour away, has a lively downtown. Yellowstone is close for a day of wildlife watching.
bigsky.know:
Bozeman airport has good winter connections and is about 1 hour away. Midwinter is very cold.

The summit tram terrain is expert-only, and some runs require avalanche gear. The Gallatin National Forest Avalanche Center covers the area.

aspen.skiing:
Four mountains on one pass: **Snowmass** (the biggest, with lots of varied terrain), **Aspen Mountain** (right above town), **Aspen Highlands** (home of the Highland Bowl, a big hike-to bowl) and **Buttermilk** (gentle, plus the parks).

It's one of the most varied destinations in Colorado, with something for every level.
aspen.beyond: Aspen is a glamorous town with excellent restaurants, galleries and shopping, and a real history as a silver-mining town. The Maroon Bells are nearby, and the X Games are held at Buttermilk each January.
aspen.know:
Aspen's own airport has direct flights but weather cancellations are common; Denver is about 3.5 to 4 hours' drive. Free buses link the four mountains.

It's expensive. Colorado's snowpack is weak and the backcountry here is serious; the Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

vail.skiing:
Vail is huge: a long, groomed front side, the open Back Bowls behind it, and Blue Sky Basin further back for trees and a more remote feel. Beaver Creek, nearby, is smaller, more polished and quieter.

The terrain suits intermediates and advanced skiers especially well; powder days in the Back Bowls are the highlight.
vail.beyond: Vail Village is built in an Alpine style, with lots of shops, restaurants and bars. Beaver Creek is known for service and its free warm cookies in the afternoon.
vail.know:
About 2 hours from Denver on I-70 in good conditions, but weekend traffic and storms can make it much longer. Eagle airport is closer.

Vail is expensive and busy at holidays. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the backcountry, which has a weak, dangerous snowpack.

summit.skiing:
Several resorts within half an hour of each other: **Breckenridge** (big, with high bowls), **Keystone** (cruisers and night skiing), **Copper Mountain** (well-separated terrain for every level) and **Arapahoe Basin** (high and steep, with a season that often runs into June).

The altitude means cold, dry snow and long seasons. Different passes cover different resorts, so check before buying.
summit.beyond: Breckenridge is an old mining town with a lively main street; Frisco and Silverthorne are cheaper bases. A-Basin is famous for tailgating in the spring sun.
summit.know:
About 1.5 to 2 hours from Denver on I-70, often much longer at weekends. Many resorts here sit near 3,000 m, so take it easy on day one and drink a lot of water.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the backcountry, which is serious.

steamboat.skiing:
Steamboat is known for its tree skiing and for its very light, dry snow, which it markets as 'Champagne Powder'. The mountain is big and rolling, with lots of intermediate terrain and excellent glades on storm days.

It's less steep than some Colorado resorts, but deep days in the trees are classic.
steamboat.beyond: A real ranching town with a Western feel, and more Winter Olympians than any other US town. The Strawberry Park hot springs are a highlight after a day on the hill.
steamboat.know:
Yampa Valley airport in Hayden is about 30 minutes away; Denver is about 3 hours by road. Midwinter is cold.

The trees here have deep snow and tree wells: ski with a partner. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the backcountry.

telluride.skiing:
Telluride sits in a dramatic box canyon in the San Juan Mountains, with a mix of long groomers for families and steep, hike-to expert terrain high on the ridges. It's rarely crowded.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America, so the expert terrain opens slowly after storms.
telluride.beyond: The old mining town of Telluride is one of the prettiest in the West, with a free gondola linking it to Mountain Village. It has a relaxed, artsy feel and good food.
telluride.know:
Remote: the small Telluride airport has limited flights; Montrose is about 1.5 hours away. It's a long drive from Denver.

The backcountry here is among the most dangerous in the US because of the weak snowpack. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers it.

crestedbutte.skiing:
Crested Butte is known for the **Extreme Limits**, some of the steepest lift-served terrain in the US: cliffs, chutes and rock bands. The lower mountain has plenty of easier skiing for families.

It's a smaller, quieter resort than the big Colorado names, and the steep terrain needs good snow coverage to open.
crestedbutte.beyond: The town is an old mining town with colourful wooden buildings and a laid-back, slightly offbeat character. It feels a long way from the bigger resorts.
crestedbutte.know:
Gunnison airport is about 30 minutes away; Denver is about 4.5 hours. The steep terrain is for experts only.

Colorado's weak snowpack makes the backcountry serious; the Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers it.

taos.skiing:
Taos Ski Valley is high, steep and sunny, with a lift to Kachina Peak and hike-to terrain along the Highline Ridge. Much of the mountain is expert terrain, though there are good beginner areas too.

It's in the far south of the Rockies, so snowfall varies a lot from year to year.
taos.beyond: The town of Taos is an art colony with adobe buildings and New Mexican food. Taos Pueblo, a UNESCO World Heritage site, has been continuously lived in for about 1,000 years.
taos.know:
About 2.5 hours from Albuquerque or Santa Fe. The base is high, at around 2,800 m, so altitude can be an issue.

The snowpack is often thin and weak; the Taos Avalanche Center covers the backcountry.

sunvalley.skiing:
Bald Mountain ('Baldy') has long, steady fall-line runs with about 1,000 m of vertical and very consistent pitch. Grooming and snowmaking are excellent; it's a mountain for skiing fast, long runs. Dollar Mountain is a separate beginner and park hill.

Sun Valley isn't known for deep powder, but the skiing is excellent.
sunvalley.beyond: Sun Valley was America's first destination ski resort, and the world's first chairlifts were built here in the 1930s. Ketchum has good restaurants and a strong literary history, including Hemingway.
sunvalley.know:
Friedman Memorial airport in Hailey is about 20 minutes away; Boise is about 2.5 hours. Sun Valley is expensive but rarely crowded.

The Sawtooth Avalanche Center covers the backcountry around Ketchum.

mtbaker.skiing:
Mt. Baker gets enormous snowfall: it holds the world record for the most snow recorded in one season. The ski area is small and old-school, with rustic lifts, but the terrain is steep and varied, with lots of natural features.

Access to the backcountry from the top of the lifts is a big part of the draw.
mtbaker.beyond: There's no lodging on the mountain; the small town of Glacier, on the road up, has a few cabins and cafés. Bellingham, about 1.5 hours away, is a lively college town.
mtbaker.know:
About 2.5 to 3 hours from Seattle. Bring everything you need: services are limited.

The backcountry here is serious: big terrain, deep snow and avalanche risk. The Northwest Avalanche Center forecasts daily. Snow can be heavy and wet, and visibility poor.

silverton.skiing:
Silverton Mountain has one chairlift and almost only expert terrain: steep, ungroomed and avalanche-controlled. In the main season you ski with a guide, in small groups; in spring, unguided days are possible. Heli drops are offered too.

Avalanche gear (transceiver, shovel, probe) is required for everyone.
silverton.beyond: Silverton is an old mining town with a lot of character and few frills. The Million Dollar Highway, linking Silverton and Ouray, is one of the most dramatic roads in the US.
silverton.know:
Durango is about 1.5 hours away; it's remote. Book guided days in advance, especially at weekends.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the area.

revelstoke.skiing:
Revelstoke has the biggest lift-served vertical in North America, about 1,700 m from the summit to the town. The terrain includes big alpine bowls, steep chutes and deep tree skiing, and the Selkirk Mountains get lots of snow.

It's also a hub for cat and heli skiing, and Rogers Pass is about an hour away.
revelstoke.beyond: Revelstoke is a small railway town with good cafés and restaurants and a relaxed, outdoorsy community.
revelstoke.know:
Kelowna airport is about 2.5 to 3 hours away; Calgary about 5 hours. Winter driving on the Trans-Canada can be challenging.

The interior snowpack often has buried weak layers. Avalanche Canada forecasts daily for the region.

kickinghorse.skiing:
Kicking Horse rises above the town of Golden, with a gondola to the summit and big alpine bowls and dozens of chutes beneath it. The terrain is steep and best for advanced skiers, with about 1,260 m of vertical.

It's part of the 'Powder Highway' route with Revelstoke and Fernie.
kickinghorse.beyond: Golden is a small working town between the Rockies and the Purcells, with access to national parks and backcountry lodges nearby.
kickinghorse.know:
Calgary is about 3 hours away by road, and Revelstoke about 1.5 hours. Winter driving through the national parks can be challenging.

The snowpack often has persistent weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

fernie.skiing:
Fernie has five big alpine bowls with lots of snow and tree skiing between them. The terrain is varied and suits intermediates and advanced skiers.

The Lizard Range catches storms and gets more snow than many nearby resorts.
fernie.beyond: Fernie is a historic coal-mining town with a lively main street and a friendly community. The Griz is the local legend said to bring the snow.
fernie.know:
Calgary is about 3 hours away; Cranbrook airport about 1 hour. Rain at the base is possible in mild storms.

The interior snowpack has buried weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

kootenays.skiing:
Two old-school ski areas with steep, deep tree skiing. **Red Mountain**, above the town of Rossland, has big glades and a lot of terrain; **Whitewater**, near Nelson, is small but has excellent snow and steep terrain.

Cat skiing operations nearby make it easy to add a day of powder skiing.
kootenays.beyond: Rossland and Nelson are small towns with real character: Nelson has an arts scene and lots of cafés and restaurants.
kootenays.know:
Castlegar airport is close but often fogged in; Spokane is about 2.5 to 3 hours away. A car helps.

The interior snowpack has buried weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

banff.skiing:
Three resorts inside Banff National Park: **Lake Louise**, big and varied with back bowls; **Sunshine Village**, high with lots of terrain and a long season; and **Norquay**, small, close to town and with night skiing.

The Rockies' snowpack is cold and dry, and the season is long. Sunshine's Delirium Dive is steep expert terrain that requires avalanche gear.
banff.beyond: Banff is a busy mountain town with hot springs, restaurants and shops. The national park's scenery is spectacular, and skating on Lake Louise is a classic.
banff.know:
Calgary airport is about 1.5 hours away by road. Midwinter can be very cold.

The snowpack often has weak layers; Avalanche Canada and Parks Canada forecast daily.

bigwhite.skiing:
Big White is a big, family-friendly resort with lots of ski-in, ski-out accommodation. The snow is dry and light, and the terrain is mostly intermediate, with good tree skiing.

The summit is often in fog, which coats the trees in rime to make the famous 'snow ghosts'.
bigwhite.beyond: A self-contained village with night skiing, tubing and activities for kids. Kelowna, in the Okanagan valley below, has wineries and lakes.
bigwhite.know:
About 1 hour from Kelowna airport. Fog and flat light are common: goggles with a low-light lens help.

Avalanche Canada forecasts for the region's backcountry.

wolfcreek.skiing:
Wolf Creek gets the most snow of any resort in Colorado. It's a family-owned ski area with simple facilities, good tree skiing and steep terrain, and lift tickets that are much cheaper than the big names.

On storm days it's one of the best places in the state.
wolfcreek.beyond: There's no lodging at the ski area: people stay in Pagosa Springs, with its natural hot springs, or South Fork. It pairs well with Taos or Telluride.
wolfcreek.know:
Pagosa Springs is about 40 minutes away; Durango about 1.5 hours. The pass road can close in storms.

The San Juans' snowpack is very weak, so the backcountry here is dangerous. The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

winterpark.skiing:
Winter Park has long cruisers for families and intermediates, and **Mary Jane** is famous for its moguls. It's one of the biggest areas in Colorado and a local favourite with Denver skiers.

The snow is often good because the resort is on the Continental Divide.
winterpark.beyond: A relaxed town with fewer frills than the big-name resorts. The Winter Park Express train runs from Denver's Union Station on weekends in season.
winterpark.know:
About 1.5 to 2 hours from Denver, over Berthoud Pass. The train is a great way to avoid I-70 traffic.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center covers the backcountry.

ogden.skiing:
Two very different resorts about an hour from Salt Lake City. **Snowbasin** hosted the 2002 Olympic downhill and has excellent, varied terrain and grand lodges. **Powder Mountain** is huge, with lots of low-angle powder, though how much terrain is open to the public has changed in recent years.

Both are far less crowded than the Cottonwood Canyons.
ogden.beyond: Ogden is a real city with a lively historic street, restaurants and a relaxed feel.
ogden.know:
About 1 hour from Salt Lake City airport. Check Powder Mountain's current ticket rules before you go.

The Utah Avalanche Center forecasts daily for the backcountry.

rogerspass.skiing:
Rogers Pass, in Glacier National Park, is one of the most famous backcountry areas in North America. The Trans-Canada Highway crosses the Selkirk Mountains here, giving road access to huge snowfall, steep old-growth trees, big alpine terrain and glaciers.

There are no lifts: it's all ski touring, from short tree laps to long glacier days and multi-day trips from the huts.
rogerspass.beyond: The Rogers Pass Discovery Centre tells the story of the railway and highway through the pass. Revelstoke and Golden are the nearest towns, both with good food and lodging.
rogerspass.know:
You need a free winter permit from Parks Canada, and some areas close on certain days for avalanche control, which uses artillery to protect the highway. Check the daily area status before setting out.

Avalanche Canada forecasts specifically for Glacier National Park. Huts are run by the Alpine Club of Canada and need booking.

bcheli.skiing:
Heli-skiing began in the Interior of British Columbia in the 1960s, and the Selkirks, Monashees and Bugaboos remain the heart of it. Operators run week-long trips from remote lodges, skiing old-growth trees on storm days and alpine glaciers when it clears. Cat skiing offers similar terrain at a lower price.

The snow is deep and frequent, and the vertical in a week can be enormous.
bcheli.beyond: The lodges are often comfortable to luxurious, with food, saunas and massage included. Many are reached only by helicopter.
bcheli.know:
This is among the most expensive skiing in the world, and popular weeks book up a year or more ahead. Cat skiing is a cheaper way in.

Operators run professional avalanche programs, but weather can ground helicopters for days. Good fitness and strong powder skiing help you get the most out of it.

tetonpass.skiing:
Teton Pass is one of the most popular road-accessed backcountry areas in the US: from the top of the pass road, tours go in every direction, from short laps to big descents. In spring, Grand Teton National Park offers serious ski mountaineering on big peaks.

The terrain is big and steep, and many slopes run onto the road below.
tetonpass.beyond: Jackson is close, with good food and a Western feel. Grand Targhee and Jackson Hole are nearby for lift-served days.
tetonpass.know:
The parking at the top of the pass fills early. Respect the road: slides can reach it, so don't trigger slopes above the highway.

The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecasts daily; the snowpack often has persistent weak layers.

tenthmountain.skiing:
A network of more than 30 backcountry huts in the Colorado Rockies between Vail, Aspen and Leadville, named after the 10th Mountain Division that trained here in World War II. Most of the touring is moderate: long approaches through forest to huts at around 3,300 m, with good tree skiing nearby.

It's more about the hut experience than big descents.
tenthmountain.beyond: The huts are cosy, with wood stoves, bunks and kitchens. Evenings with friends in a hut far from any road are the highlight.
tenthmountain.know:
Popular dates book up fast. The altitude is high, so acclimatise first. Navigation can be challenging in storms.

The Colorado snowpack is weak; the Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily.

sanjuans.skiing:
Road-accessed touring around Red Mountain Pass, between Silverton and Ouray, in the high San Juan Mountains. The terrain is big and alpine, with lots of steep slopes. Huts and yurts allow multi-day trips.

The San Juans have one of the weakest snowpacks in North America, so conservative decisions are essential.
sanjuans.beyond: Ouray has natural hot springs and a famous ice-climbing park. Silverton is a historic mining town.
sanjuans.know:
The pass road (the Million Dollar Highway) is steep and can close in storms. Silverton and Ouray are the bases.

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center forecasts daily. Going with a local guide is a good idea, especially early in the season.

cascadevolcanoes.skiing:
A spring road trip to ski the big Cascade volcanoes, such as Hood, Adams, St. Helens, Rainier and Baker. Each offers a long climb on skins and crampons, then a descent of 1,500 to 2,000 m on corn snow.

The higher peaks are glaciated, with crevasses and serious mountaineering hazards.
cascadevolcanoes.beyond: The Pacific Northwest offers great food, coffee and breweries in Portland and Seattle, and lots of camping and hot springs along the way.
cascadevolcanoes.know:
The best season is roughly May to July. Climbing permits are required on several peaks, including Rainier and St. Helens.

Glacier travel skills are essential on the higher peaks. Start early, before the snow softens too much. The Northwest Avalanche Center covers the area.

easternsierra.skiing:
Huge couloirs and open faces rise straight above Highway 395 between Bishop, Mammoth and Lone Pine. In spring, the Eastern Sierra is one of the best places in the world for corn snow on big, steep lines.

Midwinter brings big storms and powder, but spring is the classic season.
easternsierra.beyond: Natural hot springs, desert landscapes and the small towns of Bishop and Lone Pine make it a great road trip. Death Valley and Yosemite are within reach.
easternsierra.know:
The season runs roughly from January to June, with the best corn in March to May. Some peaks, like Mount Whitney, need permits.

The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Long approaches and big vertical mean early starts.

wapta.skiing:
The Wapta Icefield traverse is the Canadian Rockies' classic hut-to-hut glacier trip, off the Icefields Parkway. It links several huts, including Bow, Peyto, Balfour and Scott Duncan, across glaciers and passes over about four to six days.

The terrain is glaciated and high, with crevasses and exposure to weather.
wapta.beyond: The Icefields Parkway is one of the most scenic roads in the world. Lake Louise and Banff are close for a rest day.
wapta.know:
The main season is roughly March to May. Huts are run by the Alpine Club of Canada and need booking.

Glacier travel skills and good navigation are essential, or go with a guide. The Rockies' snowpack often has weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

sierrahr.skiing:
A committing multi-day traverse across the high Sierra Nevada near Mount Whitney, through wilderness with no huts for most of the way. It crosses high passes and alpine basins over about six to seven days.

You carry everything, camp in the snow and need strong navigation and skiing skills.
sierrahr.beyond: It's one of the wildest ski trips in the lower 48, through Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks.
sierrahr.know:
Spring (roughly March to May) is the season. A wilderness permit is required. Plan the logistics carefully: the start and finish are far apart by road.

The Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center covers the eastern side. Go with a guide unless you're experienced in multi-day backcountry travel.

shasta.skiing:
Mount Shasta is a lone volcano, about 4,320 m high, with long corn-snow descents of around 2,000 m on several sides. It's a classic spring and early-summer objective.

The climb is long and the summit high, so altitude and weather matter.
shasta.beyond: The town of Mount Shasta has a quirky, spiritual reputation. Lassen Volcanic National Park is about 1.5 hours away for more volcano skiing.
shasta.know:
A summit pass and wilderness permit are required. The best season is roughly May to June.

The Mount Shasta Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Weather on the summit can change very fast.

bclodges.skiing:
Backcountry lodges in the Selkirks, Purcells and Monashees offer a week of touring from the door. You fly in by helicopter to a timber lodge near treeline, then tour each day on terrain that ranges from tree runs to alpine bowls.

The Interior BC snowpack is deep, and the skiing is some of the best in the world.
bclodges.beyond: Lodges are cosy, with saunas and good food. The isolation, far from any road, is a big part of the appeal.
bclodges.know:
Lodges can be guided or self-guided, and catered or self-catered. Popular weeks book up a year ahead.

The interior snowpack has buried weak layers; Avalanche Canada forecasts daily.

wapass.skiing:
Each spring, the North Cascades Highway (State Route 20) reopens after winter, giving road access to steep granite couloirs and glaciers around Washington Pass. The terrain is big, steep and dramatic.

The season is short, usually from the road opening in spring until the snow melts.
wapass.beyond: The Methow Valley, with Mazama and Winthrop, has excellent cross-country skiing and a relaxed, small-town feel.
wapass.know:
The highway is closed all winter and usually reopens in spring; check the reopening date before planning. There are no services at the pass.

The Northwest Avalanche Center forecasts the area. Wet slides and cornices are the main spring hazards.

gudauri.skiing:
Gudauri sits high on the Georgian Military Highway in the Greater Caucasus, with lifts climbing above 3,000 m over wide, treeless slopes. The pistes are simple and uncrowded, but the draw is the open freeride terrain between and beyond them, plus heli-skiing at prices far below the Alps or Canada.

With no trees, storm days and flat light are hard, and the big open slopes are serious avalanche terrain.
gudauri.beyond: Georgian food and wine are a highlight of any trip: khachapuri, khinkali, and wine made in clay qvevri jars. Kazbegi (Stepantsminda), with the Gergeti Trinity Church under Mount Kazbek, is a short drive further up the highway.
gudauri.know:
Tbilisi is about 2 to 2.5 hours away by road. The highway is the main route to Russia, so expect truck traffic, and the pass above Gudauri can close in storms.

There's no full public avalanche forecast like in the Alps, and off-piste accidents happen every winter: hire a local guide. It's very good value.

svaneti.skiing:
Upper Svaneti sits under the highest peaks of the Caucasus, with mountains of 4,000 to 5,000 m. Two small ski areas near Mestia, Hatsvali and Tetnuldi, give lift access to big terrain, and from them you can tour into wild, rarely skied mountains.

The terrain is big and remote; this is a place for touring with a guide rather than a resort trip.
svaneti.beyond: The medieval stone defensive towers of Svaneti are a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Ushguli, a cluster of tower villages further up the valley, is one of the highest permanently inhabited villages in Europe. Svan food, music and hospitality make the trip.
svaneti.know:
Mestia has a small airport with flights from Tbilisi that depend on the weather; by road it's a long drive from Kutaisi or Zugdidi. Plan extra days.

There's no public avalanche forecast: go with a local guide who knows the snowpack. Facilities are simple, and English is less common than in Tbilisi.

kackar.skiing:
The Kaçkar Mountains, in Türkiye's Pontic Alps, rise steeply above the Black Sea. Moist air off the sea brings deep, heavy snowfalls onto steep, treeless ridges and gullies. Skiing here is by helicopter from lodges, in terrain that sees very few skiers.

Runs are long, with big vertical, and the snow can be deep and maritime.
kackar.beyond: The Black Sea coast below is lined with tea plantations, and the Hemşin valleys have their own distinct culture, music and food. Trabzon's Sumela Monastery, built into a cliff, is a classic side trip.
kackar.know:
Trabzon and the Rize–Artvin airport are the usual gateways. Heli-skiing here is guided and sold as weekly packages; the operator manages the avalanche risk.

Weather off the Black Sea changes quickly, so expect some down days.

gulmarg.skiing:
Gulmarg's gondola climbs to almost 4,000 m on Mount Apharwat, one of the highest lift-served points in the world. Above the trees, huge open bowls and long descents back through the forest offer some of the most affordable big-mountain freeride anywhere.

The groomed pistes are limited; Gulmarg is a freeride destination.
gulmarg.beyond: Srinagar's houseboats on Dal Lake, Mughal gardens and Kashmiri cooking (wazwan) are part of the trip. Gulmarg itself is a small hill station with simple hotels.
gulmarg.know:
Check your government's travel advice before you go: some advise against travel to parts of Jammu and Kashmir. There's a heavy security presence in the region.

Srinagar is about 1.5 to 2 hours away by road. The upper gondola often closes in wind or storms. Avalanche risk is high and there's no full public forecast, so hire a local guide.

karakol.skiing:
A small ski resort above the town of Karakol, near the eastern end of Lake Issyk-Kul, plus yurt-based touring and cat skiing in the surrounding Tian Shan. The snow is cold and dry, typical of a continental climate.

The terrain is big and open, with plenty of room for a small group to explore.
karakol.beyond: Lake Issyk-Kul never freezes, and the nearby valleys have hot springs and yurt camps. Karakol has a wooden Russian Orthodox church and a Dungan mosque built without nails.
karakol.know:
Bishkek is about 6 to 7 hours away by road. Russian is useful.

The continental snowpack often has a weak base and depth hoar, and public forecasting is limited, so go with local guides or a cat operation.

iranresorts.skiing:
Dizin and Shemshak, in the Alborz mountains north of Tehran, offer high, dry snow. **Dizin** is big and open, with lifts reaching above 3,500 m; **Shemshak** is steeper, with lots of moguls and off-piste. Both are among the highest ski areas in the region.

The skiing is surprisingly good and very cheap.
iranresorts.beyond: Tehran is a huge, busy city with museums, bazaars and parks. Iranian hospitality is famous.
iranresorts.know:
Many governments advise against travel to Iran, and dual nationals face particular risks: check your government's advice first. International bank cards don't work, so bring cash.

Dress codes and other rules apply, including on the slopes. Tehran is 1 to 2 hours away, depending on traffic.

damavand.skiing:
Mount Damavand, at 5,610 m, is the highest volcano in Asia and the highest peak in Iran. In spring, a long climb from the Bargah-e Sevom hut leads to a huge descent on snow from near the summit, where sulphur vents steam from the rocks.

The skiing itself isn't technical, but the altitude makes it a serious undertaking.
damavand.beyond: The surrounding Alborz villages are traditional and welcoming. Tehran is close for a day in the city.
damavand.know:
Many governments advise against travel to Iran: check your government's advice. Bring cash, as international cards don't work.

You'll need several days to acclimatise. Local agencies can arrange logistics, permits and mule support.

lebanon.skiing:
Lebanon's mountains get more snow than people expect. **Mzaar Kfardebian**, about an hour from Beirut, is the largest ski area; **The Cedars**, in the north, is smaller and higher, above an ancient cedar grove.

The season is short, and snow varies a lot from year to year.
lebanon.beyond: Ski in the morning and be at the Mediterranean by afternoon. Beirut's food and nightlife, Byblos and the Qadisha Valley, a UNESCO World Heritage site, are all close.
lebanon.know:
Travel advice for Lebanon changes quickly, and some areas are no-go: check your government's advice first. US dollars in cash are useful.

The roads up can close in storms. Weekends are busy with skiers from Beirut.

almaty.skiing:
A gondola from the city of Almaty climbs past the Medeu ice rink to Shymbulak, a modern ski resort in the Tian Shan. Lifts reach above 3,000 m, and the freeride terrain beyond the resort is big and steep, with a 4,000 m wall of mountains behind.

The snow is dry and continental.
almaty.beyond: Almaty is a big, green, lively city with excellent restaurants, cafés and bazaars, and prices well below Europe. Big Almaty Lake and the Charyn Canyon are good side trips.
almaty.know:
Almaty has a busy international airport, and the resort is about 30 minutes from the city. It's cheap and easy to combine city and mountains.

The continental snowpack often has a weak base: go with a local guide for off-piste. Russian is widely spoken.

almatytouring.skiing:
Multi-day ski touring in the mountains above Almaty, staying in yurts, mountain huts and an old Soviet observatory. Tours explore the Bogdanovich Glacier above Shymbulak, the Turgen Gorge and the Ketmen ridge further east.

The terrain is big and remote, with dry, continental snow.
almatytouring.beyond: Almaty is close for a city day, with good food and bazaars. Staying in a yurt is part of the experience.
almatytouring.know:
Go with local guides who know the area and the snowpack. The continental snowpack often has a weak base, and public forecasting is limited.

Russian is useful. Almaty has good international connections.

mera.skiing:
Mera Peak (6,476 m) is one of the classic Himalayan ski objectives: a long, gentle glacier descends from near the summit, with views of Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and other giants.

The skiing isn't technical, but the altitude makes everything hard, and the snow is often wind-affected.
mera.beyond: The trek in through the Khumbu and Hinku valleys is part of the trip, with Sherpa villages, monasteries and teahouses.
mera.know:
A peak permit is needed, usually arranged through a licensed agency. Expect two to three weeks, including the flight to Lukla (often delayed by weather) and acclimatisation.

The main seasons are spring and autumn. Go with an experienced operator.

annapurna.skiing:
Ski touring from the lodges at Annapurna Base Camp, inside a ring of 7,000 and 8,000 m peaks. The terrain around the sanctuary is glaciated and high, and the scenery is extraordinary.

It's more about the setting than long descents.
annapurna.beyond: The trek in passes through Gurung villages, rhododendron forests and terraced hills. Pokhara, the starting point, is a relaxed lakeside town.
annapurna.know:
Trekking permits are required. The trail into the sanctuary passes through a narrow gorge with real avalanche danger after heavy snow: check conditions with locals.

Go with an experienced operator, and leave time for weather.

muztagh.skiing:
Muztagh Ata, at 7,546 m, is often called the classic first 7,000 m peak to ski: a broad glacier slope descends from near the summit. It's an expedition of about three weeks, with several camps and acclimatisation.

The skiing isn't steep, but the altitude makes it extremely demanding.
muztagh.beyond: The Karakoram Highway and Lake Karakul below the mountain are spectacular. Kashgar's old town and bazaar are a highlight.
muztagh.know:
Xinjiang has pervasive police checkpoints and surveillance, and border areas need permits: check your government's advice first. Climbing permits go through a licensed Chinese agency.

Summer (roughly July) is the season. Go with an experienced expedition operator.

ararat.skiing:
Mount Ararat (5,137 m) is a huge volcano with a summit ice cap. In spring, a climb with camps, often with mule support, leads to a long descent on snow, with views into Iran and Armenia.

The skiing isn't technical, but the altitude is significant.
ararat.beyond: Doğubayazıt, the nearest town, is home to the Ishak Pasha Palace. The mountain is linked to the story of Noah's Ark.
ararat.know:
Ararat is in a military border zone: a climbing permit through a licensed Turkish agency is required, and it takes time. Plan well ahead.

The best season is spring. Acclimatise carefully.

altay.skiing:
The Altay region in the far north of Xinjiang has very dry, cold powder. Jikepulin is a large modern resort with long runs and new lifts, near Hemu, a village of Tuvan log cabins.

The region claims to be the birthplace of skiing, based on ancient rock paintings.
altay.beyond: Hemu's log cabins, wooden fences and frosted birch forests are beautiful in winter. Kanas Lake is nearby.
altay.know:
Xinjiang has pervasive police checkpoints and surveillance, and border areas need permits: check your government's advice first. Mobile payment apps are essential in China.

It's very cold in midwinter. Access is usually via Ürümqi and a domestic flight.

erciyes.skiing:
Erciyes is an extinct volcano (3,917 m) above the city of Kayseri, with a modern ski resort on its slopes. The terrain is wide and open, mostly intermediate, with good freeride on the volcano's flanks.

The snow is usually dry and the lifts are new.
erciyes.beyond: Cappadocia, about an hour away, has cave hotels, underground cities and hot-air balloon flights at dawn. It's an unusual combination with skiing.
erciyes.know:
Kayseri airport is about 30 minutes from the resort, with flights from Istanbul. It's good value.

There's limited avalanche forecasting, so be careful off-piste.

uzbekistan.skiing:
Amirsoy is a new resort in the western Tian Shan, about 90 minutes from Tashkent, with modern lifts and well-groomed runs. Chimgan, nearby, is older, with Soviet-era lifts and more character.

The skiing is simple and pleasant rather than challenging.
